newsitem.title: MEXICO: Mexico prides in record 1997 energy spending.
newsitem.headline: Mexico prides in record 1997 energy spending.

text.p: Mexico's President Ernesto Zedillo on Monday pledged record investments this year in energy projects to make up for years of neglect and to cater to an expected surge in economic growth.

More than 50 billion pesos have been budgetted for state oil and gas monopoly Petroleos Mexicanos (Pemex) in 1997 in a move to boost crude oil output to 3.083 million barrels per day (bpd) from an average 2.858 million bpd in 1996. Analysts have called the increase an overdue output boost.

One day before Mexico's celebrated anniversary of the day it kicked foreigners out and reclaimed the petroleum industry, Zedillo trumpeted the nation's hydrocarbon riches and expansion projects as a source of national pride.

"The energy sector will continue to be a pillar of our sovereignty, and will also continue being a pillar of our nationalism," Zedillo said at the 1997 energy program presentation at the National Institute of Nuclear Studies.
In addition to a symbol of pride, Pemex is an important source of the nation's wealth, with tax income from the petroleum giant contributing to more than a quarter of public sector revenues.

"The central objective of the energy sector in 1997 is to consolidate vigorous growth of productive activity, satisfying the fuel and electricity demands required by an expected economic growth of 4.5 percent," the government 1997 energy program read.

Energy Minister Jesus Reyes Heroles also reiterated the nation's aggressive expansion plans and investment opportunities in limited natural gas distribution and drilling and pipeline construction projects being auctioned to the private sector.

Drilling and production remains exclusively under state control, despite the gradual entry of private investment in auxiliary activites, such as distribution and petrochemical derivatives elaboration.

This time last year the government came under attack by the powerful oil workers union for attempting to fully privatize the petrochemicals sector. Union leader Sen. Carlos Romero Deschamps's outraged speech spurred the government to backtrack and tone down privatization plans.
The union holds five positions on Pemex's 11-member board of directors, and can mobilize the company's almost 130,000-member work force.
